name: CortexDynamics NeuralHelm Pilot-Rated Vehicle Link BCI
description:
The CortexDynamics NeuralHelm is a pilot-rated neural vehicle interface BCI certified for ground, air, and watercraft operation under GLMZ's Great Lakes Transit Authority Class II Neural Piloting License. The implant establishes a full sensorium merge with compatible vehicles — translating the vehicle's sensor array (proximity, inertial, environmental, mechanical stress) into proprioceptive body-sense rather than visual display, allowing the pilot to feel the vehicle as an extension of their own body with sub-20ms total latency. The NeuralHelm supports simultaneous multi-system management: a trained pilot can monitor engine load, navigation, weapon hardpoints (where licensed), cargo bay status, and atmospheric conditions as parallel sensory streams without cognitive overload, thanks to CortexDynamics' proprietary Parallel Sensory Arbitration engine. The BCI is rated for vehicles up to 85 metric tons displacement and certified compatible with over 3,400 vehicle makes including Meridian Transit Commission haulers, Axiom Aerospace short-hop craft, and the Iowan Behemoth interface collar standard for operators working alongside autonomous machines.

The NeuralHelm sits at the intersection of professional necessity and genuine subculture. Licensed pilots — courier haulers, air taxi operators, Great Lakes maritime freight crews, emergency response fliers — wear it as a trade credential, often displaying the CortexDynamics logo on their flight gear with the same pride as a union patch. But the implant has also generated a devoted enthusiast community around competitive neural racing circuits, where the quality of the merge and the pilot's ability to push sensory arbitration to its limits determines winner from wreckage. Street-level courier gangs who can't afford licensing run gray-market NeuralHelm units stripped of their GLTA certification flags, accepting the legal risk for the competitive edge the merge provides. CortexDynamics quietly tolerates this secondary market — it moves units and builds brand loyalty — while officially cooperating with GLTA enforcement inquiries.
installation_requirements: CortexDynamics certified installer or GLTA-approved neural clinic; requires Class II Neural Piloting License application or employer sponsorship; vehicle compatibility pairing session post-installation; 2-week supervised merge calibration period
rejection_risk: Low — modular electrode array adapts to varied cortical topographies; risk increases with prior vestibular system implants or inner ear modifications that conflict with proprioceptive merge signals
maintenance: Biannual vehicle compatibility database update; annual GLTA certification recalibration; electrode array inspection every 18 months; merge latency benchmark test required for license renewal
specifications: {"merge_latency": "<20ms full sensorium", "vehicle_mass_rating": "up to 85 metric tons", "simultaneous_sensor_streams": "up to 16 parallel", "compatible_vehicle_makes": "3,400+", "proprioceptive_translation_axes": "6DoF + stress/vibration", "certification": "GLTA Class II Neural Piloting", "iowan_behemoth_interface": "collar-standard compatible", "range_from_vehicle": "neural merge active within 4m proximity", "emergency_disconnect": "<50ms hard-break on pilot incapacitation", "battery": "galvanic harvest + vehicle-powered while merged"}
side_effects: Phantom vehicle syndrome — long-term pilots report persistent proprioceptive awareness of their primary vehicle even when unmerged, described as 'feeling the engine breathe' or 'knowing where the hull is' at a subconscious level

Spatial scale dysphoria during merge transitions — the perceptual shift from human-body-scale to vehicle-scale and back can cause 10-30 seconds of disorientation, particularly after extended high-stress merge sessions
Some users develop mild agoraphobia when on foot in open spaces, unconsciously missing the sensor envelope that made large environments legible while merged
Rare: merge dependency — pilots with 5+ years of heavy NeuralHelm use occasionally report that unmerged locomotion feels 'thin' or 'blind,' and seek unnecessary merge time for psychological comfort
cultural_context: In GLMZ's transit and logistics culture, a NeuralHelm pilot is a professional archetype with deep roots — the spiritual successor to the long-haul trucker, the bush pilot, the harbor captain. The implant's distinctive low-profile crown array is recognizable in any freight depot or air dock, and veteran pilots develop near-mystical reputations for their merge quality. The neural racing subculture has pushed this further, creating a folk-hero tradition around pilots who can merge so completely with a vehicle that they seem to stop being a person and become something else entirely for the duration of a run.
known_users: GLTA-licensed commercial pilots and freight haulers
Great Lakes maritime freight and ferry operators
Emergency response and medevac air crews
Gray-market courier gang pilots operating without GLTA certification
Iowan Behemoth coordination operators working alongside autonomous machines
story_hooks: A NeuralHelm pilot's merge logs show she piloted a cargo hauler through a restricted zone during a blackout she has no memory of — but the vehicle's black box confirms the merge was active and the biometrics were hers. Whatever was in that cargo has since disappeared, and people are asking questions she can't answer.

The latest CortexDynamics firmware update has introduced a subtle latency increase in the merge for a specific vehicle class — one that happens to be used exclusively by an independent freight cooperative that's been underbidding a major corporate logistics contract. It looks like sabotage from the inside, and a pilot who noticed has gone quiet.

A retired neural racing legend offers the players passage across Lake Michigan in exchange for help — but her NeuralHelm has been broadcasting a ghost signal that her old crew thinks is a message, and the people who sent it don't want it received.
